justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across horizons, starting near the current price level and gradually trending higher. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 43.45 is essentially anchored to the last observed price, with only a slight directional bias based on recent momentum or mean-reversion tendencies in the underlying asset. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate up to 43.70, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption — perhaps consistent with a slight bullish trend or carry effect. By one month, the estimate rises to 44.50, incorporating a longer-run drift assumption while acknowledging that prices tend to revert or continue trending over multi-week periods depending on the regime. In all cases, the estimates are conservative and close to the current level, reflecting uncertainty about direction rather than a strong conviction call.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which is a direct consequence of volatility compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 42.1 to 44.8 implies relatively tight bounds consistent with typical daily price fluctuations. At one week, the interval widens to 41.0–46.4, reflecting that over five trading days, a wider range of outcomes is plausible even under normal market conditions. By one month, the interval of 38.5–50.5 is quite wide, capturing the realistic possibility of meaningful directional moves in either direction over roughly 20 trading days. The interval widths were calibrated using an assumed annualized volatility level, scaled appropriately to each time horizon using square-root-of-time scaling.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macroeconomic shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, deteriorating economic data, or a geopolitical escalation — could drive prices well below 38.5 over the month. Liquidity crises or sector-specific news could also compress prices sharply within even a single day, breaching the lower bound of the one-day interval. On the upside, a strong earnings surprise, a policy pivot toward accommodation, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices above 50.5 over the monthly horizon. These tail risks are real but were not fully captured in a symmetric volatility-based framework.

Finally, it is worth noting that my framework implicitly assumes relatively stable volatility across the forecast horizon and treats the drift as approximately constant. In practice, volatility is itself uncertain and can spike dramatically — what practitioners call volatility-of-volatility — which would make all my intervals too narrow if conditions shift abruptly.
